chapter: Learning drums and trombone, New Orleans
title: City versus country musicians when he reached New Orleans
summary: Town players were smoother and more technical than country ones because of few teachers and no radio.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: We interviewed him a couple years ago. I forgot that he told us that he taught some pupils here. He probably mentioned you, no doubt. He did. I'd forgotten that. I was going to ask for how I think of it. Was there much difference in the music that you'd heard before you moved to New Orleans when you did come down here? Did the music strike you as being any better or different here than other parts of the state around outside? Well, when I first came here, I hadn't been in any

other parts of the states, because I was a kid and I came from up there where I was born. But it was different. It was different here. The boys in town were playing a little different from the boys in the country. The boys in town seemed like they were a little more smoother. They played a little more smoother, I would say. I would say they had more techniques than the boys in the country. They did. They had more techniques. Because at that time, there wasn't but a very few music teachers in the country. I suppose not many in the small towns. Very few teachers. And there wasn't very much environment, that is, in a way of musicals, for youngsters to pick up on. No, I guess not. It's hard to hear. Right. He didn't get a chance to hear many musicians. So for that cause... No radio in those days. Right. No radio or anything. Right. For that cause, he was... Well, I would say the country musician was way behind the city musician. Way behind with techniques, the music person. Such that, you know, such as modern playing, he was behind. Because there wasn't many musicians out there.
